title: Goblin Market: date, title and dedication
short: Written in April 1859 and published in 1862 as the title poem of Rossetti's first commercially published volume; first called 'A Peep at the Goblins'.
body: Goblin Market opened Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862), with frontispiece and title-page designed by Dante Gabriel Rossetti. William Michael Rossetti records that its original title was 'A Peep at the Goblins', dedicated 'To M. F. R.', their sister Maria Francesca Rossetti, and reports that Christina told him she meant nothing profound by this fairy tale, which is not a 'moral apologue'; he adds that its incidents are suggestive and that different readers will find different messages. That frankness has licensed a long tradition of readings: religious (temptation and redemption), sexual and social (the 'fallen woman'), economic (the market), feminist and psychoanalytic. The opening phrase 'Morning and evening' makes the goblins' cry habitual, part of every day.

sources.cite: W. M. Rossetti, ed., The Poetical Works of Christina Georgina Rossetti (London: Macmillan, 1904), notes, pp. 459-60

title: 'Come buy our orchard fruits, / Come buy, come buy'
short: The goblins' refrain imitates a London street-hawker's cry, and inverts Isaiah's invitation to 'buy ... without money'.
body: The cry 'Come buy' recurs throughout the poem as a refrain. It sounds like the street-cries of Victorian costermongers and fruit-sellers, and critics such as Herbert Tucker have read the goblins' patter as a parody of advertising, the 'sugar-baited words' of an expanding consumer market. It also inverts a biblical invitation: 'Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters ... yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price' (Isaiah 55:1). The prophet offers free grace; the goblins sell, and the price turns out to be the buyer's body and life. Terrence Holt and Elizabeth Campbell read the poem as an analysis of exchange and of women's place in a market economy.

title: The fruit catalogue: 'All ripe together'
short: The goblins offer fruits of every season and climate ripe at the same moment, a sign that their orchard is unnatural.
body: The opening list mixes English hedgerow fruit (crab-apples, dewberries, bilberries, damsons) with imported luxuries (oranges, lemons, pine-apples, citrons, dates, pomegranates), and fruit of spring, summer and autumn: 'All ripe together / In summer weather'. Such abundance belongs to Eden or to enchantment, and Lizzie later describes the goblin bowers 'Where summer ripens at all hours'. The incantatory list, with its tumbling rhymes and dactylic lines, is itself seductive: the reader is tempted along with Laura. The catalogue has also been read as an image of Victorian imperial commerce, which made exotic produce available to London buyers.

title: bullaces ... greengages ... barberries
short: Old English fruit names: a bullace is a small wild plum; a greengage a sweet green plum; barberries are sour red berries.
body: A bullace is a wild plum (Prunus insititia), smaller and sourer than the damson, hence 'sharp'. The greengage, named after Sir William Gage who introduced it to England in the eighteenth century, is a sweet green plum. Barberries are bright red, acid berries of the Berberis shrub, so 'Bright-fire-like'. Dewberries are a low-growing blackberry; 'Swart-headed' means dark-topped ('swart', swarthy, black). Rossetti's precise country vocabulary makes the goblin catalogue sound like a real market stall even as its abundance becomes uncanny.

title: Laura and Lizzie
short: The two sisters; Laura's name evokes Petrarch's Laura, the idealised beloved of love poetry, Lizzie is a homely diminutive.
body: The sisters are introduced in parallel ('Laura bowed her head to hear, / Lizzie veiled her blushes'), and the poem continues to set them side by side, one 'curious', the other cautious. 'Laura' is the name of Petrarch's beloved, the type of the woman praised by male sonneteers; Rossetti, of Italian family, later questioned that tradition in the preface to 'Monna Innominata'. Some critics read the name as making Laura the woman who is consumed, others as a figure of the poet-figure tempted by beauty. Many biographical readers have connected the pair with Christina and Maria Rossetti, to whom the poem was dedicated.

title: 'Who knows upon what soil they fed / Their hungry thirsty roots?'
short: Laura's own warning: the fruits' origin is unknown, and the roots that fed them are themselves 'hungry'.
body: Ironically it is Laura who first voices the danger. The question of where the fruit comes from is central to economic readings: goblin goods have no known origin and no ordinary price, so they sit outside honest exchange; the refrain 'Men sell not such in any town' says the same. The 'hungry thirsty roots' also suggest that the fruit feeds on something, perhaps on the bodies of girls like Jeanie, over whose grave 'no grass will grow'. The image of consuming and being consumed runs through the poem.

title: The goblins as animals
short: Each goblin is described by an animal likeness: cat, rat, snail, wombat, ratel, parrot.
body: The animal comparisons run through the goblins' introduction: a cat's face, a rat's face, a snail's gait, a wombat, a ratel, and a parrot's voice. Dante Gabriel Rossetti's frontispiece gave them animal heads and human bodies, fixing a reading that the poem itself leaves open. The comparisons suggest the goblins' mixed, unnatural nature and their appetite; they are also oddly comic. The poem never says what goblins are; their indeterminacy is part of their menace.

sources.cite: R. W. Crump, ed., Christina Rossetti: The Complete Poems, notes by Betty S. Flowers (Penguin, 2001), notes to Goblin Market

title: wombat ... ratel
short: A wombat is a burrowing Australian marsupial; a ratel is the honey badger of Africa and India.
body: Both animals were exotic to English readers in 1859, known from natural history books and the London Zoological Gardens, and their foreignness adds to the goblins' strangeness. The wombat 'prowled obtuse and furry' (dull, blunt); the ratel, the honey-badger (Mellivora capensis), 'tumbled hurry skurry'. The ratel's taste for honey may be apt in a poem of honeyed temptation. The Rossetti family was fond of unusual animals, and Dante Gabriel later kept a wombat at Cheyne Walk (1869), a decade after the poem was written.

title: a voice like voice of doves
short: The goblins sound gentle and loving, like doves, a deceptive comfort with biblical echoes.
body: The dove is the biblical bird of innocence, love and the Holy Spirit ('be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves', Matthew 10:16), and the Song of Songs makes the voice of the turtle-dove a sign of spring and love (2:12). Here the goblins' cooing is a disguise: they 'sounded kind and full of loves'. The gap between sound and nature recurs: their tones are 'as smooth as honey', their words 'sugar-baited'. The poem keeps asking readers, like Laura, to judge between appearance and reality, a theme with strong roots in Rossetti's devotional writing.

title: The similes of Laura's neck
short: A cluster of similes for Laura's stretching neck ends with a ship at launch, slipping its last restraint: a figure of release into danger.
body: Laura's gesture of longing is described in four similes: a swan among rushes, a lily in a beck (brook), a moonlit poplar branch, and a ship 'at the launch / When its last restraint is gone'. The sequence moves from stillness to irresistible motion: the last image makes her desire a vessel that cannot be recalled once released. Such clustered similes are a structural device of the poem, used again for Lizzie besieged ('Like a lily in a flood') and for Laura's collapse ('Like the watch-tower of a town'). Critics note how the parallel catalogues bind the sisters' stories together.

title: Brother with queer brother
short: In 1859 'queer' meant odd, strange or suspicious; the goblins leer and signal to one another like conspirators.
body: The goblins exchange looks, 'Leering at each other, / Brother with queer brother; / Signalling each other, / Brother with sly brother'. The parallel with 'sly' shows that 'queer' has its common Victorian senses: strange, of questionable character (OED). The goblins are an all-male fraternity, a parody of the sisterhood the poem praises; critics reading the poem's gender politics stress that the goblins are 'men' throughout, merchants who trade with girls. Modern readers may hear later senses of the word, but they should be distinguished from Rossetti's.

title: 'To take were to purloin'
short: Laura has no money and is honest: to take the fruit without paying would be theft. The goblins propose another price.
body: Laura's scruple shows her to be a moral agent: she knows the rules of exchange. Her only gold is the gorse flower on 'the furze / That shakes in windy weather', natural wealth that cannot be spent. The goblins' answer, 'You have much gold upon your head', turns her body into currency. Holt and Campbell see the scene as exposing how a market economy makes women's bodies objects of exchange. 'Purloin' (to steal, from Anglo-French purloigner, to put far away) is an elevated word in her plain speech.

anchor: Buy from us with a golden curl
title: the golden curl
short: Laura pays with a lock of her hair: a love-token, a piece of the self, and, many critics argue, a figure for sexual surrender.
body: A lock of hair was a familiar Victorian love-token and memento, kept in lockets; to give it was to give a part of oneself. Pope's Rape of the Lock had already made the stolen lock a mock-heroic emblem of violated chastity. Laura 'clipped a precious golden lock' and 'dropped a tear more rare than pearl', a phrase that recalls the 'pearl of great price' (Matthew 13:46). Readers concerned with the fallen-woman theme take the exchange as the loss of virginity; economic readers stress that the body has become currency.

anchor: Sweeter than honey from the rock
title: Sweeter than honey from the rock, / Stronger than man-rejoicing wine
short: The fruit's taste is described in biblical phrases for divine gifts: honey from the rock and wine that cheers man.
body: 'Honey out of the rock' is God's gift to his people (Deuteronomy 32:13; Psalm 81:16, 'with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee'). 'Man-rejoicing wine' recalls Judges 9:13, 'wine, which cheereth God and man', and Psalm 104:15. Rossetti, a devout Anglican, would know these texts well. The triple comparison (honey, wine, water) makes the goblin fruit a counterfeit of divine nourishment: it seems to surpass the gifts of God but cannot satisfy. Hence the question 'How should it cloy with length of use?', which the plot answers: it never satisfies, and never comes again.

anchor: She sucked and sucked and sucked
title: 'She sucked and sucked and sucked the more'
short: The repeated verb gives Laura's eating an infantile, sensual, compulsive intensity, much discussed by critics.
body: Laura does not eat but sucks, 'until her lips were sore', and then forgets time ('knew not was it night or day'). The insistent repetition presents appetite as compulsion. Gilbert and Gubar read the scene as an image of forbidden female desire and of the woman artist's hunger; others have compared Laura's craving and withdrawal to addiction, and Mary Wilson Carpenter discusses the poem's frank treatment of the female body and its appetites. The compulsive structure, a craving that the first taste can never satisfy, drives the plot until Lizzie's intervention.

title: one kernel stone
short: Laura keeps a fruit stone, which she later plants; it never grows. Goblin fruit is barren.
body: Laura flings the rinds away but saves 'one kernel stone'. Later, in her decline, she plants it 'by a wall that faced the south', waters it with tears, and 'hoped for a root', but 'there came none'. The seed's failure shows that the goblin fruit cannot be reproduced or possessed: it is pure consumption, without increase. The episode has been read as an image of sterility, of desire that cannot be satisfied, and, in readings concerned with sexuality, of barrenness outside marriage, contrasted with the children of the coda.

title: Jeanie
short: A girl who ate goblin fruit, pined and died: the cautionary tale of the 'fallen woman'.
body: Lizzie's warning tells of Jeanie, who took the goblins' gifts 'in the moonlight', 'pined and pined away', grew grey and died with the first snow; no grass grows on her grave. Later the poem adds that she 'should have been a bride', but 'for joys brides hope to have / Fell sick and died'. The language points to the Victorian figure of the fallen woman, who loses her chance of marriage through sexual experience. From about 1859 Rossetti worked as a volunteer at the St Mary Magdalene Penitentiary at Highgate, a refuge for such women, and critics including Jan Marsh and Mary Wilson Carpenter connect the poem with that work, though the dating of her involvement is uncertain.

title: 'Golden head by golden head ... Locked together in one nest'
short: The sisters asleep together are shown in a series of paired images: pigeons, blossoms, snowflakes, ivory wands.
body: This tender passage presents sisterly unity through doubled similes: 'two pigeons in one nest', 'two blossoms on one stem', 'two flakes of new-fall'n snow', 'two wands of ivory / Tipped with gold for awful kings' (sceptres for kings who inspire awe). Moon, stars, wind and owls guard them. The physical closeness ('Cheek to cheek and breast to breast') has invited readings of homoerotic feeling, while others stress the Victorian conventions of sisters sharing a bed and the poem's celebration of female solidarity. The scene also marks the last moment of innocence before Laura's divided state, 'One content, one sick in part'.

title: The sisters' working day
short: A picture of the ordered rural household: honey, milk, bread, butter, sewing. Laura is present but absent in mind.
body: The domestic economy of the sisters' cottage, in which goods are produced by work, not bought, is the counter-image to the goblin market. Elizabeth Campbell reads this as a female economy set against the masculine marketplace. 'Neat like bees' links them with the industrious bee of moral tradition. Yet the passage divides at once: 'Lizzie with an open heart, / Laura in an absent dream'. When Laura sickens, the poem lists the same tasks undone ('She no more swept the house, / Tended the fowls or cows'), so that her decline is measured in household terms.

anchor: To find her sister heard that cry alone
title: Laura can no longer hear the goblins
short: Once they have tasted, the goblins' victims can never hear or see them again; only the innocent Lizzie still hears the cry.
body: The poem's cruellest rule is that the first taste brings a craving for a second, but the second taste is never granted. Laura listens in vain; Lizzie, who has refused, still hears 'Come buy'. The logic is that of temptation in Christian moral writing: the sinner, once fallen, is abandoned by the tempter, and desire becomes despair. Laura 'turned cold as stone', and her questions ('Must she then buy no more such dainty fruit? ... Gone deaf and blind?') show the senses that once revelled now shut.

sources.cite: R. W. Crump, ed., Christina Rossetti: The Complete Poems, notes by Betty S. Flowers (Penguin, 2001), notes to Goblin Market

title: Her tree of life drooped from the root
short: A biblical image: the tree of life of Eden and Revelation; and Proverbs, where 'hope deferred maketh the heart sick'.
body: The tree of life grows in Eden beside the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Genesis 2:9) and again in the New Jerusalem (Revelation 22:2). Proverbs 13:12 is especially close to Laura's state: 'Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.' For Laura desire is perpetually deferred, so her tree of life droops. The phrase introduces a sequence of biblical language for her despair: she 'gnashed her teeth for baulked desire', recalling the 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' of the damned (Matthew 8:12).

title: a traveller sees / False waves in desert drouth
short: Laura dreams of melons as a thirsty desert traveller sees a mirage of water.
body: The epic simile compares Laura's fantasy to a mirage: 'False waves in desert drouth / With shade of leaf-crowned trees', which only make the traveller 'burn the thirstier in the sandful breeze'. 'Drouth' is the older form of drought. The image extends the poem's opposition between true and false nourishment, and anticipates Laura's tears later 'Dropping like rain / After long sultry drouth', when the true remedy arrives. Fantasy feeds desire and starves the dreamer.

anchor: put a silver penny in her purse
title: Lizzie's silver penny
short: Unlike Laura, Lizzie comes with real money; when the goblins refuse an honest sale, she demands her penny back.
body: Lizzie's coin turns the encounter into a test of exchange. She 'Tossed them her penny' and asks for fruit to take home; the goblins insist that she eat with them ('Honour and eat with us'), since their trade depends on consumption on the spot. When she asks for her penny back, their courtesy collapses into violence. Terrence Holt argues that the poem exposes a system in which the goblins never really sell; they take the buyer herself. The penny returned 'jingle / Bouncing in her purse' shows that Lizzie has gained without paying, an economy of gift.

title: Mopping and mowing
short: Making faces and grimacing; an old phrase found in Shakespeare.
body: To 'mop' and 'mow' is to grimace, pull faces (OED). The pair occurs in the Quarto text of King Lear (4.1), where Edgar names the fiend 'Flibbertigibbet, of mopping and mowing', and Ariel's spirits come 'with mop and mow' in The Tempest (4.1.47). The Shakespearean echo associates the goblins with devils and mischievous spirits. The surrounding passage, a cascade of present participles ('Flying, running, leaping, / Puffing and blowing, / Chuckling, clapping, crowing'), recalls nursery rhyme and shows Rossetti's virtuoso handling of short, irregular rhyming lines.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'mop'

anchor: Held her hands and squeezed their fruits
title: The goblins' assault
short: When Lizzie refuses to eat, the goblins attack her, trying to force the fruit into her mouth.
body: The scene moves from courtship to violence: they elbow and jostle her, claw, tear her gown, soil her stocking, pull her hair, stamp on her feet and squeeze fruit against her mouth. Many critics read it as a figure of sexual assault, which Lizzie survives without 'consenting'; others emphasise its spiritual sense, a martyr's ordeal. Lizzie's silence is her defence: 'Would not open lip from lip / Lest they should cram a mouthful in'. Her passive endurance is presented as heroism, which Dorothy Mermin calls a form of heroic sisterhood.

anchor: Like a lily in a flood
title: Lizzie's similes: 'a royal virgin town'
short: Lizzie under attack is a lily, a rock, a beacon, an orange-tree, and finally a besieged virgin city that will not lower its flag.
body: This set of similes balances the earlier ones for Laura. Lizzie is 'White and golden' like a lily in floodwater, a blue-veined rock lashed by tides, a beacon sending up fire in a storm, an orange-tree (its blossom the traditional bridal flower) beset by wasps, and 'a royal virgin town / Topped with gilded dome and spire / Close beleaguered by a fleet / Mad to tug her standard down'. The last image draws on the old allegory of chastity as a besieged castle, as in the siege of Alma's castle in Spenser's Faerie Queene (2.11). 'Obstreperously' (noisily, unruly) is a deliberately heavy word in a rhythmic line.

sources.cite: Spenser, The Faerie Queene 2.11

anchor: One may lead a horse to water
title: 'One may lead a horse to water'
short: A proverb, comically abrupt after the heroic similes: force cannot make Lizzie eat.
body: 'A man may well bring a horse to the water, but he cannot make him drink' is recorded in John Heywood's collection of proverbs (1546). Rossetti alters it ('Twenty cannot make him drink'), fitting the goblin crowd. The sudden drop from epic simile to homely proverb is typical of the poem's mixture of registers: nursery verse, fairy tale, biblical echo and moral fable. It also states the poem's ethic plainly: the will that refuses cannot be compelled.

anchor: Eat me, drink me, love me
title: 'Eat me, drink me, love me'
short: Lizzie offers herself to Laura in words that echo Christ's at the Last Supper, making her a female saviour figure.
body: Lizzie returns smeared with juice and cries 'Hug me, kiss me, suck my juices ... Eat me, drink me, love me'. The words echo the Eucharist: 'Take, eat; this is my body ... Drink ye all of it' (Matthew 26:26-27) and 'Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life' (John 6:54). Lizzie, who has suffered for her sister, becomes a type of Christ; readers since Marian Shalkhauser (1956) have spoken of a 'feminine Christ', and Dorothy Mermin and Victoria Coulson discuss the poem's redemptive language. The bodily intensity of the scene has also invited erotic readings, and Mary Wilson Carpenter takes the phrase for the title of her essay. The two readings need not exclude each other.

title: the fruit forbidden
short: Laura names the goblin fruit as the forbidden fruit of Eden, making her own fall a repetition of Eve's.
body: The phrase recalls Genesis 3 and the first line of Paradise Lost, 'Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit / Of that Forbidden Tree'. Laura fears that Lizzie too has fallen ('Undone in mine undoing, / And ruined in my ruin'), the language of the fallen woman. The Eden pattern runs through the poem: the tempting fruit, the 'tree of life', the expulsion into a barren world. The redemption that follows is not by a male saviour but by a sister, which many feminist critics take as the poem's most daring revision of the story.

anchor: That juice was wormwood to her tongue
title: wormwood
short: Wormwood is a proverbially bitter plant; in the Bible it stands for bitterness, suffering and judgment.
body: The same juice that was 'Sweeter than honey' now tastes of wormwood (Artemisia absinthium). In the KJV wormwood figures affliction: 'He hath filled me with bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood' (Lamentations 3:15), and in Revelation 8:11 a star named Wormwood makes the waters bitter. The reversal is the cure: the antidote is the same fruit, now loathed. Laura 'gorged on bitterness without a name', and her frenzy ('Writhing as one possessed') recalls Gospel scenes of exorcism, where the demon tears its victim before leaving (Mark 9:26).

anchor: Like the watch-tower of a town
title: Laura's fall: the collapse similes
short: Laura's collapse is described in images of catastrophe: tower, mast, tree and waterspout falling.
body: The final cluster of similes mirrors Lizzie's: where Lizzie stood like a besieged town, Laura falls 'Like the watch-tower of a town / Which an earthquake shatters down', a lightning-struck mast, an uprooted tree, a waterspout 'Cast down headlong in the sea'. Before that, her hair streams like a racer's torch, a horse's mane, an eagle flying into the sun, a freed caged thing, a flag when armies run. The two sets of similes, for liberation and for ruin, make the crisis both a death and a release. The passage ends with a question: 'Is it death or is it life?'

sources.cite: R. W. Crump, ed., Christina Rossetti: The Complete Poems, notes by Betty S. Flowers (Penguin, 2001), notes to Goblin Market
Dorothy Mermin, 'Heroic Sisterhood in Goblin Market', Victorian Poetry 21.2 (1983)

title: 'Life out of death.'
short: A one-line paragraph answers the question just asked: Laura's crisis is a death that brings new life, the pattern of Christian resurrection.
body: The short line, set apart, turns the poem. Its idea is the Pauline and Johannine paradox: 'Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit' (John 12:24); 'that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die' (1 Corinthians 15:36). Lizzie's vigil through the night leads to a dawn of reapers and 'golden sheaves', harvest imagery that contrasts with the barren goblin kernel. Laura wakes 'as from a dream', her grey hair gone golden again. Coulson reads the poem's language of salvation as central rather than ornamental.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), John 12:24
Bible (KJV), 1 Corinthians 15:36
Victoria Coulson, 'Redemption and Representation in Goblin Market: Christina Rossetti and the Salvific Signifier', Victorian Poetry 55.4 (Winter 2017), 423-50

title: The coda: wives and mothers
short: Years later both sisters are married mothers; Laura tells the children the story. The husbands are never seen.
body: The coda moves the tale into the past, as a story told to children. Critics have long noticed that the husbands are absent: the only men in the poem are goblins, and the household is still the sisters' world. Some readers find the ending a conventional retreat into marriage and motherhood; others, notably Gilbert and Gubar and later feminist critics, emphasise that the story's moral is about sisters, not spouses. Laura's words recall the poem's own refrain: the merchants' fruits were 'like honey to the throat / But poison in the blood', and Lizzie won 'the fiery antidote'.

sources.cite: Sandra M. Gilbert and Susan Gubar, The Madwoman in the Attic (Yale, 1979), ch. on Rossetti
Dorothy Mermin, 'Heroic Sisterhood in Goblin Market', Victorian Poetry 21.2 (1983)
Elizabeth Campbell, 'Of Mothers and Merchants: Female Economics in Christina Rossetti's Goblin Market', Victorian Studies 33.3 (1990)

anchor: Men sell not such in any town
title: '(Men sell not such in any town)'
short: A parenthetical refrain, first used of the goblins' crown of nuts and repeated in the coda: goblin goods are outside ordinary trade.
body: The line appears twice in parentheses, first when a goblin weaves Laura a crown 'Of tendrils, leaves, and rough nuts brown', and again when Laura tells the children of the 'wicked, quaint fruit-merchant men'. Its point is that goblin wares are not part of the honest market: they cannot be bought in any town, and their price is not money. Terrence Holt took the line as the title of his influential study of exchange in the poem. The recurrence also binds the coda to the opening, as if the storyteller's voice were the narrator's.

sources.cite: Terrence Holt, "'Men sell not such in any town': Exchange in Goblin Market", Victorian Poetry 28.1 (1990), 51-67
Herbert F. Tucker, 'Rossetti's Goblin Marketing: Sweet to Tongue and Sound to Eye', Representations 82 (2003)

anchor: there is no friend like a sister
title: 'For there is no friend like a sister'
short: The closing moral praises sisterly love; it recalls the dedication to Maria Rossetti and the proverb of a friend closer than a brother.
body: The poem ends with a moral fit for children, set to a ballad-like rhythm: a sister will cheer, fetch, lift and strengthen. Proverbs 18:24 speaks of 'a friend that sticketh closer than a brother', and Rossetti feminises the idea. The original dedication 'To M. F. R.' (Maria Francesca Rossetti) gives it a personal resonance, and the story's central action is Lizzie's saving of Laura. Dorothy Mermin reads the poem as a myth of heroic sisterhood. The very simplicity of the last lines, after so much sensuous and violent writing, has been read both as resolution and as a deliberate understatement.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Proverbs 18:24
Dorothy Mermin, 'Heroic Sisterhood in Goblin Market', Victorian Poetry 21.2 (1983)
